newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola to bring in unity government, seal peace.
newsitem.headline: Angola to bring in unity government, seal peace.

text.p: Angola's former foes form a power-sharing government on Friday, marking the official end of nearly two decades of fighting which practically destroyed the southern African country.

The national unity government comes into being after many postponements, delays and a shaky 1994 peace treaty intended to end the civil war which broke out between Jonas Savimbi's UNITA and the MPLA government on independence from Portugal in 1975.
Angolan President Jose Eduardo dos Santos reappointed Fernando Franca Van Dunem as prime minister to head the new "Unity and National Reconciliation Government", which will include UNITA members.
One of the biggest stumbling blocks to bringing UNITA into the reconciliation process was finding a job for Savimbi, who refused to serve as a deputy president to dos Santos.

This week the Angolan parliament cleared away that hurdle by passing a law giving Savimbi the title "president of the largest opposition party", a post that carries such privileges as the right to consult dos Santos and live in an official residence in Luanda.

But it is not certain if Savimbi will attend the swearing-in ceremony on Friday, although a time slot has been left for him to speak. Savimbi, who is based in the central highlands town of Bailundo, has said he is not confident of his safety in Luanda.

The president of the former colonial power Portugal, Jorge Sampaio, has arrived to attend the ceremony and South African President Nelson Mandela is expected. Russia and the United States are among other countries represented.

A stable, lasting peace in Angola should allow greater exploitation of the country's largely unexplored mineral wealth and could bring greater regulation to diamond mining, now largely the realm of freelancers under UNITA control.
Aid agencies hope peace will pave the way for revitalisation of agriculture, although millions of anti-personnel mines still need to be cleared from vast tracts of the country.

But diplomats in Luanda cautioned against greeting formation of the new government with excessive optimism. They noted a major problem would be extending central government administration to remote parts of the country dominated by UNITA where the war has left the infrastructure in tatters.
"The negotiations on extension of state administration are moving very slowly," said one official close to the peace process. "The issue could very well be a major problem."
U.N. officials this week unveiled a plan to begin demobilising some 40,000 UNITA fighters on Saturday. The soldiers have spent months in U.N. assembly areas.
About 6,000 U.N. peacekeepers have helped monitor the demobilisation process since the two sides signed a peace pact in Lusaka in November 1994.
The pact took root despite sceptism engendered by the failure of an earlier peace accord in 1991 that led to elections but was quickly snuffed out by a return to war.
Tens of thousands of Angolans died during the war and millions were displaced.
